result: The study optimized peptide extraction methods from wound fluids by comparing three buffer conditions (urea alone, urea + RapiGest, urea + TFA) and found that 100 µL of wound fluid in 6 M urea supplemented with 0.05% RapiGest yielded the highest number of unique peptides (3543) and was selected for further studies.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 provide clear experimental evidence from Figure 1 showing systematic comparison of extraction buffers and volumes. The selection of urea + RapiGest is justified by quantitative data showing superior peptide recovery compared to other methods.

result: The selected sample preparation method demonstrates robustness with 62% protein overlap and 58% peptide overlap when splitting samples across filters, high reproducibility across multiple injections on the same day, and stability during storage at 4°C.
evaluation: Claims C38-C43 are supported by systematic reproducibility testing shown in Figure 2, including filter comparison, injection reproducibility, and storage stability. The data demonstrate acceptable technical variability for the method, though the 58% peptide overlap (C39-C40) indicates some filter-related losses.

result: Wound fluids contain substantially more peptides than plasma from healthy donors, with over 5 times as many proteins and 6.8 times as many peptides. Wound fluids show enrichment in smaller peptides (700-1500 Da), higher post-translational modifications (6.4% vs 3.1% deamidation, 21.7% vs 4.5% methionine oxidation), and presence of protease-derived peptides absent in plasma.
evaluation: Claims C44-C54 are strongly supported by comprehensive comparative analysis shown in Figure 3, including SDS-PAGE, LC-MS/MS chromatograms, quantitative peptide counts, size distribution, and modification analysis. The data clearly demonstrate the proteolytic nature of wound fluids versus healthy plasma.

result: Analysis of five sterile acute wound fluids identified 2649-4271 peptides per sample corresponding to 373 total proteins, with 74 proteins common to all samples. The 74 common proteins yielded 783 identical peptides (15% of total), and average peptide length varied from 12.3 to 13.7 amino acids, suggesting different levels of proteolytic activity.
evaluation: Claims C55-C61 are supported by data in Figure 4 and Supplementary files showing comprehensive peptidome characterization across multiple wound fluid samples. The variation in peptide length (C60-C61) provides indirect evidence for differential proteolytic activity, though direct protease measurements would strengthen this inference.

result: Comparison of three normally healing surgical wounds versus three S. aureus-infected inflamed wounds showed that infected wounds had higher cytokine levels (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α), increased protein degradation and enzymatic activity, and higher peptide-to-protein ratios (52 vs 34 peptides per protein), indicating elevated proteolytic activity. Infected wounds also showed greater inter-patient variability.
evaluation: Claims C62-C75 are well-supported by multi-modal analysis in Figure 5 including clinical photos, cytokine measurements, SDS-PAGE, zymograms, and comprehensive peptidomics. The higher peptide-to-protein ratio in infected wounds (C70-C71) provides quantitative evidence for increased proteolysis, consistent with known biology of infected wounds (C72).

result: Specific proteins showed differential presence between wound types: complement C9 was only detected in infected wounds, dermcidin was present in healing wounds but absent in infected wounds (likely due to bacterial degradation), and lactoferrin was only detected in infected wounds (consistent with neutrophil degranulation).
evaluation: Claims C76-C84 are supported by heatmap data in Figures 5 and 8. The differential protein detection patterns are consistent with known biology: C9 in bacterial defense (C77), dermcidin degradation by staphylococci (C80-C81), and lactoferrin from neutrophils (C83-C84). The biological interpretations are well-supported by citations.

result: Peptide profiling of coagulation and inflammatory proteases revealed distinct fragmentation patterns: fibrinogen-derived peptides including antimicrobial GHR28 (intact in healing wounds, fragmented in infected wounds), thrombin light chain peptides (present in healing, absent in infected), thrombin-derived C-terminal peptides (TCPs), and cathepsin G/elastase fragments (enriched in infected wounds) including known antimicrobial regions.
evaluation: Claims C85-C98 are strongly supported by detailed peptide mapping in Figure 6 showing specific fragmentation patterns. The identification of known bioactive peptides (GHR28, TCPs, CG-1) with appropriate citations (C86, C90-C91, C95-C96) and their differential presence in wound types provides compelling evidence for protease-specific degradation patterns.

result: Peptide profiling of protease inhibitors revealed specific fragmentation patterns: HMWK-derived peptides including bradykinin-containing D4 domain and antimicrobial D5 domain fragments; A1AT C-terminal fragments with immunomodulatory potential; antiplasmin C-terminal regions (only in healing wounds) with urokinase-modulating activity; and ITIH4 peptides from the proline-rich region (residues 488-504 unique to healing wounds).
evaluation: Claims C99-C117 are supported by peptide mapping data in Figure 7 with appropriate structural and functional context from citations. The differential detection of specific peptide regions (e.g., antiplasmin C-terminal in healing wounds C111, ITIH4 488-504 in healing wounds C117) provides evidence for wound-type-specific proteolytic processing.

result: Complement system peptides showed specific patterns: Factor B S1 peptidase domain fragments in infected wounds, C3a N-terminal peptides with antimicrobial activity, C3b opsonin fragments, and two CO3 peptide sequences unique to healing wounds. Serum amyloid A-1 C-terminal fragments were found in non-infected wounds, suggesting proteolytic processing with potential physiological roles.
evaluation: Claims C118-C131 are supported by peptide mapping in Figure 8. The identification of complement activation products (C121-C124) and SAA fragments (C129-C130) is well-documented. However, the proposed physiological role of SAA fragments (C131) is speculative and appropriately marked as such.

result: Additional wound-specific peptide patterns were identified: dermcidin DCD-1L variants with N-terminal SSLLEK in healing wounds; fetuin-A connecting peptide region with distinct N-terminal sequences differentiating inflamed (LPPAGS) from non-inflamed (LLAAPP) wounds; and highly similar albumin fragmentation patterns across samples demonstrating method robustness.
evaluation: Claims C132-C140 are supported by peptide mapping in Figure 8. The identification of DCD-1L variants (C134) and fetuin-A N-terminal differences (C138-C139) between wound types provides potential biomarkers. The albumin consistency (C140) serves as an internal control validating the method.

result: This study developed a novel peptidomics workflow for wound fluid analysis that characterized over 7800 peptides from more than 370 proteins in acute wound fluids, representing the first comprehensive characterization of the human wound fluid peptidome using mass spectrometry.
evaluation: Claims C4, C8, and C144 accurately describe the methodological contribution. The workflow is clearly documented in Figure 1, and the comprehensive peptide identification is supported throughout the results. The novelty claim (C4) is reasonable given the focus on endogenous peptides rather than tryptic digests.

result: The study demonstrates proof-of-concept that wound fluid peptidomics can detect qualitative differences in peptide patterns between patient groups and provides potential biomarkers for wound healing and infection, though validation in larger cohorts is needed.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C145 are supported by the comparative analysis of healing versus infected wounds showing distinct peptide patterns. However, the small sample size (n=3 per group) and the speculative nature of biomarker potential (C10) appropriately limit this to proof-of-concept rather than validated biomarkers.

result: The wound fluid peptidome serves as a source for assessing wound dynamics, with peptide fragments representing proteolytic events from coagulation, complement activation, and endogenous/bacterial protease activities.
evaluation: Claims C142-C143 are supported by the comprehensive peptide profiling showing fragments from coagulation factors, complement components, and protease-specific cleavage products. The interpretation that these reflect physiological processes is well-supported by the data and established biology.

result: Peptidomics findings at the peptide level (thrombin, dermcidin, lactoferrin, fibrinogen) correspond to previous proteomic observations by Eming et al. 2010. Subsequent bioinformatics analysis (Hartman et al. 2021) identified enrichment of acidic residues at P1 position, specific C-terminal sequences in infected wounds, and predicted neutrophil elastase upregulation in infected samples.
evaluation: Claims C158-C165 appropriately cite supporting evidence. The correspondence with Eming et al. (C158) validates the peptidomics approach. The bioinformatics findings (C159-C165) are properly attributed to Hartman et al. 2021, demonstrating the utility of the generated datasets for further analysis.

result: The authors propose that combining peptide biomarkers with classical cytokine/MMP analyses could improve diagnostic sensitivity and specificity for wound status, and that antibody/aptamer-based sensors targeting selected peptides could enable clinical translation. The peptidomics data may aid discovery of novel bioactive peptides.
evaluation: Claims C175-C176 and C178 are appropriately speculative about future applications. While the proof-of-concept data support the potential utility, no validation studies, sensor development, or functional characterization of novel peptides are presented. These remain hypotheses requiring substantial additional work.
